title: Asymmetric KV Shard + Kernel Fusion Scheduling Notes
content:
Context and motivation:

This note collects experiments and heuristics around an asymmetric KV sharding approach combined with coarse-grained kernel fusion for transformer attention (prefetch + attn compute + writeback) on GPUs. Goal is to reduce end-to-end p95/p99 latency for production tail requests where long contexts and mixed sequence lengths cause KV fetch variability, while keeping throughput degradation minimal for batchy steady-state traffic.

Key ideas summarized:
- Shard KV across multiple memory pools (fast local device memory, near-term pinned host staging, and multi-page persistent GPU-backed slab). The asymmetry: small, recent context lives in an L0 fast slab; older or less-likely tokens are stored in L2-like pages with on-demand fetching.
- Fuse kernel boundaries where beneficial: prefetch + copy + a portion of attention computation in a single cooperative launch to hide PCIe/HBM copy latency and reduce kernel launch overheads for short-lived requests.
- Scheduling policy that prefers coalescing requests targeting the same shard/page into a micro-batch window (few ms) but falls back to single-request fast-paths when latency SLO is tight.
- Per-request priority hints used to break ties for eviction and to decide whether to invoke fused launches or lean on standard, high-throughput kernels.

Design details:

1) Asymmetric KV layout and addressing
- L0 slab: contiguous device-resident hot KV vectors (prefetched or recently used). Sized small per-stream (e.g., 8-64 MB depending on model). Quick lookup table: per-session circular offsets.
- L1 staging: pinned host pages used as staging for larger but still somewhat-recent context. Asynchronous DMA from pinned host to device when a request expects to reuse the page soon.
- L2 pages: large cold-backed allocation (sized by page size e.g., 4MB–16MB) kept in CUDA unified memory or device-backed slab with on-demand transfers.

Address translation: compact two-byte shard identifier + 3-byte page offset + 3-byte token offset (example packing for 8B alignment). The runtime maintains a small LRU+frequency sketch per shard to steer prefetch actions.

2) Prefetch+Compute Fusion pattern
- Standard flow (no fusion): kernel A prefetches KV for tokens -> host/device memcpy -> kernel B runs attention -> kernel C writes updated KV back. Each kernel launch costs CPU overhead and kernel scheduling latency.
- Fused flow idea: combine steps A+B into a single launch where warps cooperatively perform staged DMA (via cudaMemcpyAsync + pinned staging segments) then immediately consume prefetched KV in register/shared memory to execute the attention microtile. The fused kernel ends with either writing updated KV directly into device L0 or staging it for an async writeback.

Implementation sketch (conceptual pseudocode):
- Each streaming multiprocessor (SM) reserves a cooperative team assigned to a page.
- Team executes: issue async DMA of page chunk -> wait on per-team event -> load chunk into shared memory/prefetch buffers -> run attention microtile over incoming tokens -> optionally compress/quantize and write back to target slab.

Pros: fewer launches, better overlap of copy and compute, lower p95 for single-request flows.
Cons: increased register/shared memory usage per SM, complexity of cooperative scheduling, less flexible for very large micro-batches.

3) Scheduling heuristics and micro-batch coalescing
- Two-path scheduler: fast-path and coalescing-path.
  - Fast-path: for requests with remaining latency budget < X ms (tunable, default 6ms), schedule into a per-GPU single-request fused launch if the targeted KV fits into L0 or a single-page staging. No cross-request coalescing.
  - Coalescing-path: for requests with slack >= X ms, hold up to N requests that touch overlapping shards/pages for up to W ms (e.g., 2–8 ms) and issue a batched fused launch that services multiple requests with shared page prefetched once. The batching window W adapts to observed arrival rates.

- Decision factors: per-request sequence length distribution, overlap score (how many tokens touch the same page), deadline slack, model quantization format, and whether attention is causal or full (non-causal often permits more re-use).

4) Eviction and priority hints
- Each request carries a priority hint: interactive | streaming | background. Priority influences:
  - whether its KV is promoted to L0 after compute (interactive yes, background maybe not),
  - eviction weight when L0 needs space,
  - whether to take the fast-path fused launch or go to the coalescing window.
- Eviction policy: hybrid frequency-weighted LRU with segment-level aging. We also maintain a tiny Bloomish frequency counter per session to avoid thrashing for very bursty sessions.

5) Memory placement and compression options
- When writing back KV from fused kernels, optionally apply 4-bit quantization + per-page scale offsets to reduce L2 footprint.
- Use packing-friendly layouts for L0 (interleaved head-major layout) to improve coalesced access in attention kernels.

6) Kernel-level optimizations
- Cooperative warp fetch: assign contiguous token vectors to warp lanes, use global memory vector loads for aligned segments, and fallback to scatter loads for tail pieces.
- Staged shared memory tiles sized to trade off occupancy vs. per-team buffering. For models with many heads and small head dim, prefer more shared memory per-team and lower occupancy; for large head-dim, keep shared minimal and rely on register tiling.
- Prefetch stride tuning: empirically choose a stride that aligns with page fragmentation to maximize DMA unit utilization while avoiding unnecessary work for unreferenced tokens.

7) Safety, fallbacks, and telemetry
- Fused kernels should support a conservative fallback mode that disables DMA overlap on GPUs where async copy semantics are not reliable (older runtimes). A runtime feature flag can disable fusion per-instance.
- Instrumentation to record: per-request path (fast/coalescing/fallback), per-shard hit rates, fused-kernel occupancy, average DMA wait time, and p50/p95/p99 improvement delta.

8) Experiments so far (summary of microbenchmarks)
- With a small toy model (8-head, 64 head-dim), fused-kernel single-request latency decreased p95 by ~22% on A100 for sequences with 4k tokens when the L0 hit rate was >= 40%.
- Coalescing-path with W=4ms and N<=12 showed throughput uplift (~1.15x) when arrival patterns had high shard overlap; tail latency improved for medium SLO classes but worsened slightly for smallest SLO classes unless we constrained fast-path.
- Writing quantized 4-bit back to L2 reduced L2 traffic by ~2.6x but added ~1.5ms CPU-side quant/dequant overhead in current prototype; moving quantize into fused kernel avoided CPU overhead at the cost of increased kernel registers.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- How to pick W dynamically across mixed workloads (prod traffic mixes interactive chat with long-run embedding pipelines)? We probably need a controller that monitors per-queue miss rates and adjusts W to balance p95.
- Eviction knobs: should we expose session-level retention guarantees for enterprise customers (pin top K MB)? This interacts with contract rules for Dedicated/Private deployments.
- Fault isolation: fused cooperative kernels that lock SMs for multi-ms can increase interference for other GPU work. Need a throttling mechanism at the scheduler level to avoid long SM occupancy saturation.
- Observability: what minimal metrics are needed to diagnose fusion regressions (e.g., per-kernel stall reasons, sm-occupancy histograms)?

Next steps / concrete action items:
- (Rafael) prototype cooperative fused kernel in branch kv-fusion-proto: implement per-team DMA + microtile attention and a simple fallback path.
- (Priya) build synthetic workload generator that can produce mix of shard overlap patterns and sequence length distributions.
- (Ethan) extend runtime scheduler to support two-path fast/coalesce policy and basic W auto-tuner based on recent hit-rate/latency tradeoffs.
- (Maya) add telemetry spec for fused-kernel feature including the key events and histograms described above; prepare short doc for infra gating and a rollout plan for Dedicated clusters.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally sketchy; we want feedback on ergonomics of the two-path scheduler and the idea of asymmetric memory semantics. In particular, comments requested on the eviction weighting scheme and whether pinned host staging is acceptable for our Private deployments (network policy, security).

Appendix: quick list of configuration knobs for experimentation (defaults in parentheses)
- L0 size per-stream (32MB)
- Page size for L2 (8MB)
- Fast-path threshold X ms (6ms)
- Coalesce window W (adaptive, start 4ms)
- Max coalesce count N (12)
- Quantize threshold for writeback (>=512 tokens)
- Fusion enable flag (false)

End of note.
